### What the message means

When you run `git push`, Git checks whether your local branch is **ahead** of the remote branch that it will update.  
The message you’re seeing:

```
Updates were rejected because the tip of your current branch is behind
its remote counterpart. If you want to integrate the remote changes,
use 'git pull' before pushing again.
```

is telling you that:

* The branch on the remote repository (e.g., `origin/main`) has commits that you **do not** have locally.
* Git refuses to overwrite those remote commits with your push because that would discard work that someone else (or you on another machine) has already pushed.

In short, your local branch is **behind** the remote. You need to bring it up‑to‑date before you can push your own changes.

---

## How to fix it

### 1. Pull the remote changes first

```bash
git pull origin main   # replace `main` with your branch name
```

This does two things:

1. **Fetch** the latest commits from `origin/main`.
2. **Merge** (or rebase, if you configure it) those commits into your local branch.

If the merge is clean, you can now push:

```bash
git push origin main
```

### 2. Use rebase instead of merge (optional)

If you prefer a linear history, you can replace the default merge with a rebase:

```bash
git pull --rebase origin main
```

or set it as the default for your branch:

```bash
git config branch.main.rebase true   # for `main` branch
```

After rebasing, push as usual.

### 3. Force‑push (use with caution)

If you *really* want to overwrite the remote history (e.g., in a feature branch that only you work on), you can force push:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease origin main
```

> **Warning:** This rewrites history on the remote. Anyone else pulling that branch will have to reconcile the divergence.

---

## Why it happens

- **Collaborative work:** Someone else pushed new commits to the remote branch after you last fetched.
- **Detached or stale local state:** You cloned a repo, then switched branches or didn’t fetch recently.
- **Rebasing / rewriting history locally:** Your local commits were rewritten (e.g., `git rebase`) and now differ from the remote’s history.

---

## Quick checklist

| Step | Command | What it does |
|------|---------|--------------|
| 1 | `git fetch` | Get latest refs from remote (no merge) |
| 2 | `git status` | See how many commits you’re behind (`behind 3`) |
| 3 | `git pull` or `git pull --rebase` | Integrate remote changes |
| 4 | Resolve conflicts if any (edit files, `git add`, then `git commit` or continue rebase) |
| 5 | `git push` | Push your updated branch |

---

## Common pitfalls

- **Conflicts during merge/rebase:** Git will stop and ask you to resolve them. Edit the conflicted files, `git add <file>`, then either commit (merge) or `git rebase --continue`.
- **Multiple remotes:** If you have more than one remote (e.g., `origin`, `upstream`), make sure you’re pulling from the correct one.
- **Stale branch name:** If your local branch is tracking a different remote branch, adjust with `git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/main`.

---

### TL;DR

1. **Pull** the remote changes (`git pull` or `git pull --rebase`).  
2. Resolve any conflicts that arise.  
3. **Push** again (`git push`).

That will sync your local branch with the remote, letting you push without rejection.

## 1. Fetch the latest refs (but don’t merge)

```bash
# Update your local copy of all remote branches, but keep your working tree untouched
git fetch origin
```

After this command you have a new *remote‑tracking* branch called `origin/<branch>` (e.g. `origin/main`).  
This is the exact state that lives on GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket, so you can inspect it without touching your local branch.

---

## 2. Look at the commit history

### a) Show a short log of what’s new on `origin/main`

```bash
git log --oneline ..origin/main   # commits reachable from origin/main but not in your current branch
```

- `..origin/main` means *“all commits that are on origin/main but not in my current branch”*.
- `git log --oneline` gives you a concise, one‑line summary of each commit.

If you’re on `main`, the command is equivalent to:

```bash
git log --oneline main..origin/main
```

### b) Show a full diff of the changes

```bash
git diff main..origin/main   # shows line‑by‑line differences between the two branches
```

If you want to see only what’s changed in the last commit on `origin/main`:

```bash
git diff origin/main~1..origin/main   # or simply `git show origin/main`
```

---

## 3. Inspect a specific file or folder

```bash
git diff origin/main -- path/to/file.txt
```

This prints the differences for that file between your current branch and `origin/main`.

---

## 4. Use a graphical view (if you prefer)

Many GUIs let you compare branches:

- **Gitk** (command line GUI):

  ```bash
  gitk main..origin/main
  ```

- **GitKraken / Sourcetree / GitHub Desktop** – just open the repo and select *Compare* or *Pull Requests* view.

- **GitHub/GitLab web UI** – navigate to the branch on the website, click *Compare*, and you’ll see a list of commits & diff.

---

## 5. Quick “what changed?” cheat sheet

| Purpose | Command |
|---------|---------|
| List new commits (one‑line) | `git log --oneline ..origin/main` |
| Full commit messages | `git log ..origin/main` |
| Show diff of all new commits | `git diff main..origin/main` |
| Diff a single file | `git diff origin/main -- <file>` |
| See last commit on remote | `git show origin/main` |

---

### Example workflow

```bash
# 1. Make sure you’re on your branch
git checkout main

# 2. Fetch the latest refs from origin
git fetch origin

# 3. See what new commits exist on the remote
git log --oneline ..origin/main

# 4. If you want a visual diff
git diff main..origin/main

# 5. Merge or rebase (after reviewing)
git pull   # or `git pull --rebase`

# 6. Push your changes
git push origin main
```

That’s it—now you can see exactly what the remote branch contains before deciding how to integrate those changes.

<|start|>assistant<|channel|>final<|message|>

## What the hint means

When you run `git pull` and Git tells you:

```
You have divergent branches and need to specify how to reconcile them.
```

it means:

* Your local branch has commits that the remote doesn’t have **and**
* The remote branch has commits that your local one doesn’t.

Git can resolve this in two common ways:

| Strategy | Resulting history |
|----------|-------------------|
| **Merge** (`git pull` → `git merge`) | Creates a new *merge commit* that ties the two histories together. |
| **Rebase** (`git pull --rebase`) | Rewrites your local commits on top of the remote ones, producing a *linear* history. |

You need to tell Git which strategy you prefer **before** the next `git pull`.

---

## How to set your preference

### 1. For a **single repository** (affects only this repo)

```bash
# Merge (the default behavior if you don’t change anything)
git config pull.rebase false

# Rebase
git config pull.rebase true

# Or require a fast‑forward only (no merge or rebase)
git config pull.ff only
```

### 2. For **all repositories** on your machine

Add the `--global` flag:

```bash
git config --global pull.rebase false   # merge everywhere
# or
git config --global pull.rebase true    # rebase everywhere
```

### 3. Override on a **per‑command** basis

If you want to override the global setting for just one pull:

```bash
# Rebase this single time
git pull --rebase

# Merge (explicitly) even if you set rebase globally
git pull --no-rebase

# Fast‑forward only (error if not possible)
git pull --ff-only
```

---

## Choosing the right strategy

| Scenario | Recommended |
|----------|-------------|
| You’re collaborating on a shared feature branch where you want to keep the history readable and avoid rewriting public commits | **Merge** (`pull.rebase false`) |
| You’re working on a personal feature branch that nobody else uses, and you want a clean linear history | **Rebase** (`pull.rebase true`) |
| You only ever want to fast‑forward (no merge commits, no rebasing) | **Fast‑forward only** (`pull.ff only`) – this will error if the histories diverge |

---

## Quick cheat‑sheet

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `git pull` | Pull + merge (default) |
| `git pull --rebase` | Pull + rebase |
| `git pull --no-rebase` | Explicitly merge, even if global is rebase |
| `git pull --ff-only` | Only fast‑forward; fails if diverged |
| `git config pull.rebase true/false` | Set repo‑level default |
| `git config --global pull.rebase true/false` | Set machine‑wide default |

---

### Example workflow

```bash
# 1. Decide you want a linear history on this branch
git config pull.rebase true

# 2. Pull the latest changes
git pull   # this will now rebase automatically

# 3. Resolve any conflicts, then continue
git add <conflicted files>
git rebase --continue

# 4. Push your rebased branch
git push origin main
```

That’s all you need to do to tell Git how it should reconcile divergent branches!

## Why this can happen even when you’re the only one working

Even if you are the sole developer, a branch can become “behind” for a few reasons:

| Situation | What happened | Typical cause |
|-----------|---------------|---------------|
| **You pushed from another machine** | You worked on your laptop, committed & pushed. Later you clone the repo to a new machine and try to push again without pulling first. | Different devices, forgetting to pull before pushing. |
| **You rebased locally and pushed** | You had a commit on `main`, rebased it onto the latest remote, then pushed. The remote now has that commit *plus* your old one (which was rewritten). Git sees the remote’s tip as “ahead” because it contains commits you don’t have locally. | Rebasing & pushing without syncing the remote first. |
| **You performed a force‑push earlier** | You rewrote history (e.g., `git push --force`) on the remote, and then later made new commits locally that are not on the remote. | Force‑push can leave the remote in a state that looks “ahead” of your current local tip. |
| **Another user (e.g., a teammate or CI) pushed** | Even if you think you’re the only one, a bot or CI job might have updated the branch. | Automatic deployments, GitHub Actions, etc. |

So the “behind” message is simply telling you: *the remote branch contains commits that your current local branch does not have*.

---

## How to fix it

1. **Fetch the latest state**

   ```bash
   git fetch origin          # updates all remote‑tracking branches
   ```

2. **Inspect what’s new on the remote**

   ```bash
   # Show commits that exist on origin/main but not locally
   git log --oneline ..origin/main

   # Show a diff of those commits
   git diff main..origin/main
   ```

3. **Integrate the remote changes**

   Choose one of these options:

   | Option | Command | Result |
   |--------|---------|--------|
   | **Merge** (creates a merge commit) | `git pull` or `git merge origin/main` | Keeps both histories, adds a merge commit |
   | **Rebase** (linear history) | `git pull --rebase` or `git rebase origin/main` | Reapplies your commits on top of the remote ones |
   | **Fast‑forward only** (no merge) | `git pull --ff-only` | Only works if your local branch has no unique commits |

   Since you’re the only one working, *rebase* is often the cleanest choice:

   ```bash
   git pull --rebase   # or: git rebase origin/main
   ```

4. **Resolve any conflicts** (if they arise)

   ```bash
   # Edit the conflicted files, then:
   git add <file>
   git rebase --continue    # if you rebased
   ```

5. **Push your updated branch**

   ```bash
   git push origin main
   ```

---

## Quick “one‑liner” if you’re sure you want to overwrite the remote

> **⚠️ Use with caution** – this rewrites history on the remote and will discard any commits that are not in your local branch.

```bash
git push --force-with-lease origin main
```

`--force-with-lease` is safer than `--force`; it refuses to push if the remote has moved since your last fetch.

---

## Bottom line

- **Behind** → The remote branch has newer commits that you don’t have locally.
- **Fix** → `git fetch` → inspect → merge/rebase → push.

Once you’ve pulled (merged or rebased), your local branch will be up‑to‑date, and the “Updates were rejected” error will disappear.

### What happened

You **force‑pushed** a rewritten history to the remote.  
That means:

```
origin/main   <-- new commit chain (your rewrite)
local main    <-- old commit chain (what you had before the force‑push)
```

Git now sees *two* different histories that share only a few common ancestors.  
When you try to push again, it refuses because the remote is “ahead” of your
local tip.

---

## Two safe ways to bring your local branch back in sync

### 1. Re‑apply your current work on top of the new remote history  
*(recommended if you have local commits that you want to keep)*

```bash
# 1. Make sure the remote refs are up‑to‑date
git fetch origin

# 2. Rebase your local commits onto the rewritten remote branch
git rebase --onto origin/main <common‑ancestor> main
```

- `origin/main` – the new tip on the remote.
- `<common‑ancestor>` – usually the commit where you originally diverged (Git can often figure this out automatically if you just run `git rebase origin/main`).

If the rebase stops for conflicts, resolve them:

```bash
# After editing conflicted files:
git add <file>
git rebase --continue
```

When the rebase finishes, your local branch will be a linear continuation of
`origin/main`.  Now you can push:

```bash
git push origin main          # no force needed, fast‑forward is fine
```

### 2. Reset your local branch to exactly match the remote  
*(use this if you truly don’t need any of the old local commits)*

```bash
# 1. Update your remote refs
git fetch origin

# 2. Hard‑reset your branch to the remote tip
git reset --hard origin/main

# 3. Push (normal push, no force)
git push origin main
```

`reset --hard` discards *all* local changes and commits that are not in
`origin/main`.  It’s the quickest way to “undo” the divergence.

---

## How to find the common ancestor (if you want more control)

```bash
git merge-base main origin/main
```

This prints the SHA of the most recent common commit.  You can then use that in
the rebase command:

```bash
git rebase --onto origin/main <common‑ancestor> main
```

---

## What to remember

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| You have local commits you want to keep | `git fetch`, then `git rebase origin/main` (or the more explicit `--onto` form) |
| You don’t need any old local commits | `git fetch`, then `git reset --hard origin/main` |
| You accidentally force‑pushed and now want to *undo* that push | `git reset --hard origin/main` on the remote machine, then `git push --force-with-lease` (only if you’re sure nobody else has pulled that state) |

---

### Quick one‑liner to keep everything local

If you’re sure your current branch is exactly what you want and you just need
to sync the remote:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease origin main   # only if you really need to overwrite the remote
```

> **Caution:** `--force-with-lease` will replace the remote history with
> whatever you have locally.  Use it only when you’re certain no one else is
> relying on the previous remote state.

---

**Bottom line:**  
- *Pull (rebase) your local commits onto the new remote history* if you want to keep them.  
- *Reset hard to the remote* if you’re fine discarding the old local history.

Pick the approach that matches your intent, and the “behind” error will be gone.
